pedagogy.summary: Mentally adding or subtracting ones to a three-digit number rests on one insight: only the ones digit changes, UNLESS the calculation bridges a ten (then the tens digit changes too, and possibly the hundreds). Children apply their secure within-20 bonds at the end of a larger number, keeping the hundreds and tens as an untouched 'anchor'. It is taught with place-value apparatus and a number line so the local change is visible against the stable larger part.
bestPractices: Anchor the hundreds/tens and operate only on the ones — 345+7 keeps '34_' fixed and works 5+7
Reuse within-20 make-ten bonds for the bridging cases (345+7 = 345+5+2 = 350+2)
Contrast a non-bridging case (345+3) with a bridging case (345+7) so the child notices when more than the ones digit changes
Use a marked number line / hundred-square segment to show the small jump near a decade
Ask the child to predict which digits will change before calculating (DfE evidence: explain that only the ones digit changes unless bridging)
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart / Gattegno chart (only the ones row moves; bridging cascades)
Number line segment around the nearest ten
Base-ten blocks (add/remove ones, exchange at the ten)
commonMisconceptions: Changing the wrong digit (adding the ones to the tens or hundreds digit)
Failing to bridge: 345+7 given as 342 or 3412 (keeps 2, drops the extra ten) instead of 352
Smaller-from-larger on the ones when subtracting bridges down (462−5 given as 463: does 5−2)
Believing 'only the ones digit ever changes', so bridging cases are mishandled

learn.summary: Year 3 pupils mentally add or subtract ones to a three-digit number. The core insight: only the ones digit changes UNLESS the calculation bridges a ten, in which case the tens digit (and possibly the hundreds) also changes. Children anchor the hundreds and tens as a stable 'larger part' and operate only on the ones, reusing secure within-20 make-ten bonds for the bridging cases. Contrasting a non-bridging case directly with a bridging case is what refines the rough rule 'only the ones change' into the accurate 'only the ones change unless we cross a ten'.

activities.title: Anchor the larger part, spin only the ones
feedback: If the child changes the wrong digit (e.g. gives 345+3 as 375, adding to the tens): re-anchor with the chart — the 3 is three ones, so it joins the ones. Name the value of each digit before adding.
Reinforce by asking which column the added amount belongs to, every time, until anchoring is automatic.
activities.rationale: Anchoring the larger part and operating only on the ones makes the local nature of the change explicit; naming place value directly counters the wrong-digit error. A coded or physical chart where only the ones row moves makes this concrete, while base-ten blocks, a bead string or a partitioning jotting (345 = 340 + 5) show the same stable-anchor idea in other media.
learnerActions: Show 345 on a place-value chart (e.g. a Gattegno chart) with the hundreds, tens and ones rows visible.
Work 345 + 3: change only the ones from 5 to 8, keeping '34_' fixed, and say aloud which digits stayed the same and which changed.
Name the value of each digit before adding (the 3 you add is three ones, so it joins the ones), to guard against adding to the wrong column.
Predict, before calculating, which digits will change.
activities.intendedInsight: A change to the ones stays local: the hundreds and tens act as an untouched anchor, so for a non-bridging case only the ones digit moves.

activities.title: Bridge a ten with make-ten bonds
feedback: If the child fails to bridge (e.g. 345+7 given as 342, keeping the 2 and dropping the extra ten, or strings digits as 3412): rebuild with make-ten on the number line — 345 to 350, then +2 — and connect it to the within-20 bond they already know.
Highlight that keeping the tens digit at 4 cannot be right because the answer passed 350.
activities.rationale: Bridging reuses within-ten make-ten bonds, and multiple representations (number line, hundred-square, place value, symbolic) connect the mental strategy. Showing the ones filling to the decade then the remainder makes visible why the tens digit moves. The cascading chart and number-line toggle are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required apparatus.
sourceClaims: Bridging a ten reuses within-ten 'make ten' bonds; multiple representations (number line, place value, symbolic) connect the mental strategy.
learnerActions: Work 345 + 7 on a marked number line (or a hundred-square segment near the decade): jump +5 to land on 350, then +2 more to reach 352.
Connect this to the within-20 bond already known: split 7 into 5 + 2, so 345 + 7 = 345 + 5 + 2.
Notice the moment the tens digit changes (4 becomes 5 as you cross 350) — this is the exception to 'only the ones change'.
Optionally watch a place-value chart where the ones roll past 9 and cascade a carry of +1 into the tens, with a number-line toggle showing the same jump onto 350 then stepping to 352.
activities.intendedInsight: When a calculation crosses a ten, the ones 'fill up' to the next decade and the tens digit also changes; make-ten bonds the child already knows handle the split.

activities.title: Contrast non-bridging and bridging side by side
feedback: If the child insists only the ones can ever change, point to the bridging case where the tens visibly moved past a decade, and ask them to re-predict.
Praise correct predictions that name the crossing of a ten as the reason the tens digit changes.
activities.rationale: Contrasting a non-bridging case with a bridging case isolates exactly when more than the ones digit changes, which is the heart of this skill. Prediction-before-calculation surfaces the misconception for discussion. Rapid mixed items can rehearse and check the skill but mainly confirm rather than build the insight.
learnerActions: Place 345 + 3 and 345 + 7 next to each other and predict, for each, which digits will change before calculating.
Calculate both, then state which digits actually changed and why they differed.
Articulate the refined rule: 'only the ones change, unless we cross a ten'.
Try a mixed set of items sorted by whether they bridge, predicting each time.
activities.intendedInsight: Directly comparing a case where only the ones change with one that bridges turns the rough rule into the accurate rule and exposes the 'only the ones ever change' overgeneralisation.

activities.title: Bridge downwards when subtracting
feedback: If the child does 'five take two is three' and gives 463 (subtracting the smaller from the larger within the column): show on the number line that 462 − 5 must move down past 460 — take 2 to reach 460, then 3 more. Sanity-check that subtracting makes the number smaller.
Reinforce the direction check as the first move on any subtraction that bridges.
activities.rationale: The smaller-from-larger error can produce an answer larger than the start, as with 462 − 5 → 463, though not always (464 − 7 → 463). A number-line model travelling down past the decade corrects it. A direction check, plus a check that the tens digit dropped, catches it. Answers across the set: 345+3 = 348 (only ones change), 345+7 = 352 (bridges up, tens change), 462−5 = 457 (bridges down, tens change).
sourceClaims: Bridging a ten reuses within-ten 'make ten' bonds; multiple representations (number line, place value, symbolic) connect the mental strategy.
learnerActions: Work 462 − 5 on a number line (or hundred-square segment near the decade), moving DOWN: take 2 to reach 460, then 3 more to land on 457.
Check direction first: subtracting should make the answer smaller than 462, so an answer above 462 is wrong.
State which digits changed (the tens digit drops from 6 to 5) and why.
Thinking aloud, do 345 + 3, 345 + 7 and 462 − 5 in turn, saying which digits change after each.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtracting across a decade moves the number down past the ten, so the tens digit drops. A direction check catches the smaller-from-larger error when it gives an answer above the start (462 − 5 → 463), but it cannot catch every case. Checking that the tens digit dropped, because the answer passed below 460, makes the check complete.

constraints: The target is mental calculation: apparatus (place-value/Gattegno chart, number line, hundred-square segment, base-ten blocks, bead string, partitioning jottings) are scaffolds to make the local-versus-bridging change visible, to be faded as the child calculates reliably in their head.

Multiple-choice or rapid mixed items (e.g. 345+7 with a 342 distractor) chiefly check whether the child bridges and catch the 'only ones change' overgeneralisation; they do not by themselves build the bridging insight, which needs the child to construct and explain the steps.
A static tap-to-reveal chart can show which digit changes but does not let the child follow the carry cascade; pair it with a number line or manipulation if the bridging mechanism is the goal.
Prerequisites: secure within-20 make-ten bonds and confident place-value naming of hundreds/tens/ones digits; reteach these if the wrong-digit or no-bridge errors persist.
Partial mastery looks like handling the non-bridging case and bridging only with a number line or apparatus, not yet reliably in the head, and possibly missing direction on subtraction.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The second listed source (NCETM make-ten bonds / multiple representations) is marked verified:false in the source row; treat its support as provisional.

sourceClaims were trimmed so each cites a source only where it supports the teaching principle: the DfE claim establishes the Year-3 objective/topic but does not support the specific anchoring, contrast or direction-check techniques, so those activities carry []. The NCETM claim is retained on the two bridging activities; note its support for the subtraction direction-check specifically is partial (it backs bridging via number line, not the direction heuristic itself).

The source row's worked subtraction note contained a garbled fragment ('462−52 wait — take 2 to reach 460, then 3 more = 457'); the intended method is take 2 to reach 460 then 3 more to 457. The corrected steps are used in the activity; the original garble is recorded here only.
Self-audit of arithmetic: 345+3=348, 345+7=352, 462−5=457 all confirmed. The distractors named (342, 3412, 463, 467) are explicitly error patterns, not valid answers.
The source claim '3D adds nothing' for this topic has been omitted as a catalog-ranking judgement rather than an established pedagogical law; this rewrite neither asserts nor relies on it.

probeDeeper: For 345 + 3, which digits changed and which stayed the same? Why?
For 345 + 7, why did the tens digit change when it didn't for 345 + 3?
Is your answer to 462 − 5 bigger or smaller than 462? Should it be?
What would 345 + 7 be if it were 345 + 70 instead — which digit changes then?
assess.correctAnswer: 348, 352, 457. 345+3 changes only the ones (348). 345+7 bridges: ones fill to 350 then +2 = 352 (tens digit also changes). 462−5 bridges down: 462−52 wait — take 2 to reach 460, then 3 more = 457 (tens digit changes).

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes the wrong digit — adds the ones amount to the tens or hundreds ('345 + 3 is 375')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor with the place-value chart: the 3 is three ones, so it joins the ones. Name the value of each digit before adding.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The altered digit is not the ones; the child adds to the wrong column

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to bridge — '345 + 7: five and seven is twelve, so 342' (keeps the 2, drops the extra ten) or 3412
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild with make-ten on the number line (345+5 to 350, then +2); connect to the within-20 bond they already know.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 345+7 the answer keeps 2 in the ones but the tens digit is unchanged, or digits are strung together

errorPatterns.pattern: Smaller-from-larger when subtracting bridges down — '462 − 5: five take two is three, so 463'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show on the number line that 462−5 must move DOWN past 460; take 2 to reach 460, then 3 more. Sanity-check direction: subtracting makes it smaller.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 462−5 the child does 5−2 and the answer is larger than the start, or the tens digit doesn't drop

responseLevels.gap: Changes the wrong digit, or gives 342/3412 and 463; believes only the ones digit ever changes.
responseLevels.full: Answers all three mentally, anchoring the larger part, bridges the ten in both directions, and explains that only the ones change unless the calculation crosses a ten.
responseLevels.partial: Handles the non-bridging case and can bridge with a number line or apparatus, but not yet reliably in his head; may miss the direction on subtraction.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to do these mentally, thinking aloud: 345 + 3, then 345 + 7, then 462 − 5. After each, ask which digits changed. Watch the two that bridge a ten.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 345+3 confirms the child anchors the larger part. 345+7 and 462−5 both bridge a ten — a child who believes only the ones digit ever changes gives 342/3412 or 467/463, while a child who bridges correctly adjusts the tens. The contrast between the non-bridging and bridging items isolates the misconception.
